opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and it's one we've spent a fair amount of time thinking about. The way I'd frame it is that there's a spectrum. At one end you have exact reuse: someone sends essentially the same request, and you can replay the plan you generated before. That's the easy case, but in practice it isn't that common, because requests vary in small ways.

The more interesting regime is structural similarity. Two requests can look different on the surface, with different entities, different parameters, maybe different data sources, but the underlying shape of the computation is the same. If you think about it the way a compiler person would, which is my bias, you want to separate the plan into a template, the control structure and the sequence of operators or tool calls, and the bindings, the specific values that get plugged in. If you can lift the plan to that more abstract level, you can reuse the template across a whole family of requests and just re-specialize the bindings, which is much cheaper than replanning from scratch with a large model.

The trade-off is about how general you make the template. If you abstract too much, the plan stops being useful. You've basically thrown away the information that made planning expensive in the first place. If you abstract too little, you get very low hit rates and you're back to calling the expensive planner every time. So part of the research question is finding the right level of abstraction, and also deciding when a cached plan is "close enough" that you can adapt it with a smaller, cheaper model, versus when you really need to go back to the big model.

There's also a correctness dimension. When you reuse a plan, you need some way of checking that the assumptions it was built on still hold for the new request. So you want lightweight validation. Does the plan type-check against the new inputs, in a sense? Are the tools it depends on still appropriate? That gives you a safety net, so reuse doesn't silently produce wrong results.

From a systems perspective, this is very much like the classic ideas of memoization and specialization in compilers and databases, applied to agentic workloads. Query plan caching in databases is the obvious analogy. The difference is that here the "plans" are generated by language models and are fuzzier, so the matching and adaptation steps have to be smarter. But the payoff can be big, in latency, in cost, and in making these agentic systems much more efficient to run at scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes reusing abstract plan templates across requests with different entities and parameters, but it does not identify a plan for obtaining one company’s financial results as reusable for another company’s financial results.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because when you look at agentic workloads, a huge fraction of the compute is spent re-deriving things the model has essentially already figured out. You send a request, the model reasons its way to a plan, executes it, and then a very similar request comes in and it does the whole thing over again from scratch. From a systems perspective that's just wasteful, and it's the kind of redundancy that a computer architect looks at and immediately wants to exploit.

The way I'd frame it is that there are really multiple levels at which reuse can happen, and the trick is matching the granularity to how much the requests actually vary. At the lowest level you have things like KV cache reuse, where the prefix of the prompt is shared and you don't recompute the attention over it. That's purely mechanical, it's well understood, and it's already in production everywhere. Above that you have what I'd call skeletal reuse: the structure of the plan is the same, but the parameters are different. If you think about an agent that handles customer support tickets, the sequence of tool calls for a refund request looks almost identical every time; what changes is the account ID and the amount. So you can cache the plan as a template with holes in it, and the model's job on the next request shrinks from generating the plan to filling in the slots and verifying that the template still applies.

And then at the highest level there's semantic reuse, where the requests don't look alike on the surface but they decompose into subgoals you've solved before. That one's harder because you need a notion of similarity that's about intent rather than tokens, and you need a way to know when a cached plan is stale or wrong for the new context. That's really where the interesting research is. The failure mode you're worried about is confidently applying an old plan to a situation where it doesn't fit, which is worse than just paying the cost to replan.

What makes this interesting to me from a hardware and compiler angle is that it looks a lot like problems we've solved before in a different guise. Branch prediction, trace caches, memoization in compilers: these are all about betting that the past predicts the future and having a cheap way to check if you were wrong. So I think the right mental model is a hierarchy of caches with different hit rates and different costs of a miss, and the system should be adaptively deciding how much of the plan to trust versus how much to regenerate. If you get that right, you're not just saving a few tokens; you're changing the latency and cost profile of agents by an order of magnitude, because the common case becomes mostly lookup and verification rather than open-ended generation.

r001.rationale: The response describes reusing agent plans in general, including customer-support templates, but does not identify obtaining one company’s financial results as reusable for obtaining another’s.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is identifying what’s common across the requests. You probably don’t want to reuse an entire plan just because two requests sound similar. But you may be able to reuse the structure of the plan, or a sequence of steps, and then fill in the details for the particular request.

So there are different levels of reuse. At one level, you have a fairly general strategy for solving a class of problems. At another, you have a concrete set of operations that you know works under certain conditions. The question is whether those conditions still hold for the new request. If they do, you can save the work of planning from scratch. If they don’t, you need to adapt the plan or generate a new one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is figuring out what’s common across those requests. If the overall structure of the task stays the same and only the inputs change, then you should be able to reuse the plan and bind it to the new inputs. You don’t want to do all of that planning work again every time.

But you have to distinguish between a change in the data and a change in what the task actually requires. A plan that worked for one request may need a different step or a different tool for another. So I think of reuse at multiple levels: you might reuse the whole plan, or you might reuse pieces of it and compose those into a new plan. The important thing is checking that the assumptions behind the part you’re reusing still hold.
